2021_215_2_a_2021_troy_letter_to_the_boa.paragraph: Plante & Moran, PLLC issued this draft Report to the Board of Education of Troy School District on October 5, 2021, communicating results of its audit of the district's financial statements for the year ended June 30, 2021 plus informational items on Michigan school finance. The auditors report no disagreements with management, no significant difficulties, and no new accounting policies, and identify the district's share of MPSERS net liabilities, estimated at $308,094,061 for pension and $48,088,931 for OPEB, as the most sensitive estimates. General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000, lifting fund balance to approximately $32,700,000, or 19.88 percent of expenditures.
2021_215_2_a_2021_troy_letter_to_the_boa.page:
**Document.** Draft "Report to the Board of Education," Troy School District, June 30, 2021, prepared by Plante & Moran, PLLC and dated October 5, 2021. Signed by Donna Hanson, CPA (Partner) and Michael Walsh, CPA (Manager). Organized as Results of the Audit (pages 1-6) and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The firm thanks Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the business office for their assistance.

**Audit scope and communications.** The engagement letter is dated June 2, 2021; planning matters were discussed with the board on August 13, 2021. The audit was conducted under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards and Government Auditing Standards, with a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 on internal control over financial reporting and compliance. A federal program audit under 2 CFR Part 200 was also completed, reported separately on October 5, 2021. Management representations are contained in a letter dated October 5, 2021.

**Significant audit findings.** No new accounting policies were adopted and no existing policies changed during 2021. No transactions lacked authoritative guidance; none were recorded in a different period than they occurred. The most sensitive estimates were the district's shares of the MPSERS net pension and OPEB liabilities under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75, estimated at $308,094,061 and $48,088,931 respectively as of June 30, 2021, based on Office of Retirement Services data. Disclosures were judged neutral, consistent, and clear. Management corrected all identified immaterial misstatements. There were no disagreements with management and no difficulties in performing the audit.

**State aid background.** The May 2020 Revenue Estimating Conference suggested proration of roughly $685 per pupil; by the August 2020 conference the actual proration for 2019-2020 was $175 per pupil. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at 2019-2020 levels, with a target foundation of $8,529, a minimum of $8,111, and a one-time $65 per pupil payment not folded into the formula. A one-year "super blend" pupil count weighted the 2019-2020 count at 75 percent and the 2020-2021 count at 25 percent. For 2021-2022 the target foundation rises to $8,700 per pupil, with a $171 per pupil increase for districts already at or above target; for hold harmless districts such as Troy the increase is expected as $115 of foundation allowance plus $56 of Section 20m funding. Counts return to 90 percent fall / 10 percent spring weighting.

**Retirement and federal relief figures.**

| Item | Amount |
| --- | --- |
| Section 147a1 | $1,070,809 |
| Section 147a2 | $1,838,621 |
| Section 147c1 | $11,658,202 |
| Section 147e | $206,687 |
| Coronavirus Relief Fund available | $4,588,959 |
| ESSER I award | $246,411 |
| ESSER II estimate | $843,258 |
| ESSER III estimate | $1,893,840 |
| ESSER II state equalization payment | $5,036,199 |

The 2020-2021 MPSERS contribution rate ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent, and from 20.96 to 28.21 percent net of state support; total contributions represent about 42 percent of covered payroll with roughly 28 percent borne net by the district. For 2022 the overall rate is expected to rise to 43 percent from 42 percent with the net share near 28 percent. CRF distributions were approximately $362 per pupil; the award was fully expended in fiscal 2021. The ESSER II funding floor was $450 per pupil and the ESSER III floor $1,093 per student, the latter now questioned by the federal government.

**MPSERS plan status.** At September 30, 2020 the plan's net pension liability was approximately $35 billion, up from $33.8 billion at September 30, 2019, an increase of about 3.5 percent. The net OPEB liability was approximately $5.4 billion, down from $7.3 billion, a decrease of about 26 percent, reflecting a health care cost trend rate reduction from 7.5 percent to 7.0 percent and favorable plan experience.

**Fund balance.** General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000 in 2020-2021, increasing General Fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The statewide average at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent of expenditures, equal to about eight weeks of operations; Troy's percentage is 19.88 percent, about 10.3 weeks.

**Forward-looking items.** Recommendations cover grants management risk assessment, budgeting for nonrecurring federal aid with program end dates laddered through 2024, cybersecurity (the "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act" introduced in the House in June 2021 would appropriate $10M yearly for two years), IT assessment, GASB Statement No. 87 on leases effective for the June 30, 2022 statements, SAS No. 134 changing the auditor's report for June 30, 2022, and the GASB financial reporting model exposure draft with phased adoption at June 30, 2025 for districts with revenue over $75 million and June 30, 2026 for those under. The next Revenue Estimating Conference is set for January 2022.
2021_215_2_a_2021_troy_letter_to_the_boa.verbose:
Plante & Moran, PLLC prepared this draft "Report to the Board of Education" for Troy School District covering the fiscal year ended June 30, 2021. The transmittal letter and each substantive letter within it are dated October 5, 2021. The report is divided into Results of the Audit (pages 1-6) and Informational Items (pages 7-19). The firm extends thanks to Mr. Rick West, Ms. Kandice Moynihan, and the entire business office for their assistance and preparedness during the audit, noting that audit preparation is carried out in addition to normal daily activities. The letter is signed by Donna Hanson, CPA, Partner, and Michael Walsh, CPA, Manager.

**Responsibility and scope.** As stated in the engagement letter dated June 2, 2021, the auditor's responsibility under U.S. generally accepted auditing standards is to express an opinion on whether the financial statements prepared by management with board oversight are fairly presented in all material respects in conformity with U.S. generally accepted accounting principles. The audit provides reasonable, not absolute, assurance that the statements are free of material misstatement and does not relieve the board or management of their responsibilities. Internal control was considered solely to determine audit procedures, not to provide assurance on internal control. The audit was also conducted in accordance with Government Auditing Standards issued by the Comptroller General of the United States, under which the firm must communicate matters involving compliance with laws, regulations, contracts and grant agreements, instances of error or fraud, illegal acts applicable to government agencies, and significant deficiencies in internal control; a separate letter dated October 5, 2021 was issued on internal control over financial reporting and tests of compliance. The audit followed the planned scope and timing communicated at the planning meeting of August 13, 2021.

**Significant audit findings.** Management is responsible for the selection and use of accounting policies, which are described in Note 2 to the financial statements. No new accounting policies were adopted and the application of existing policies was not changed during 2021. No transactions were entered into for which there is a lack of authoritative guidance or consensus, and no significant transactions were recognized in a period different from when they occurred. The most sensitive accounting estimates were the School District's share of the MPSERS net liabilities for the pension and other postemployment benefit (OPEB) plans recorded on the government-wide statements under GASB Statement Nos. 68 and 75. As of June 30, 2021 those estimates were $308,094,061 for pension and $48,088,931 for OPEB, based on data received from the Office of Retirement Services. Disclosures are described as neutral, consistent, and clear. No significant difficulties were encountered, no disagreements with management arose, management corrected all immaterial misstatements identified, and there were no consultations with other independent accountants. A federal program audit required by 2 CFR Part 200 was completed, with results reported separately on October 5, 2021. Management representations are included in a letter dated October 5, 2021. The firm read the Annual Comprehensive Financial Report and found nothing materially inconsistent with the financial statements. The information is intended solely for the Board of Education and management.

**Informational items - state aid background.** The report frames the period as "A Year Like No Other" and traces the move "From 18 Months of Financial Uncertainty to Projected Stability." Before the pandemic, state resources were stable and predictable. In spring 2020 substantial proration of state aid was feared, prompting two Revenue Estimating Conferences, the scheduled May 2020 conference and an additional August 2020 conference. The May conference suggested proration estimated at $685 per pupil, and many districts adopted final 2020 budget amendments on that basis; by August 2020 the actual proration for the 2019-2020 fiscal year was set at $175 per pupil. Beginning in March 2020 the federal government provided several waves of assistance with evolving spending requirements, though COVID-19 relief funds ultimately allowed more flexibility than traditional federal grants. For 2020-2021 the foundation allowance was held at the 2019-2020 level, no prorations were required, and a $65 one-time per pupil payment was provided; the State also supplemented districts that did not reach a minimum per pupil threshold from the Educational Stabilization Fund. For 2021-2022 all schools move to a target foundation allowance of $8,700 per pupil, eliminating the equity gap between base and target, and all districts including hold harmless districts receive at least a $171 per pupil increase, with added funding for special education, At-Risk, wraparound services such as nurses and counselors, and the Great Start Readiness Program (GSRP), reflecting School Finance Research Collaborative recommendations.

**2021 funding implications for Troy.** Because of pandemic-related concerns, 2020-2021 foundation levels were maintained at 2019-2020 levels: the target foundation allowance (formerly the basic foundation allowance) was $8,529 and the minimum foundation allowance remained $8,111, with the one-time $65 per pupil payment excluded from the formula and not retained for 2021-2022. For 2020-2021 a one-year "super blend" pupil count combined the 2019-2020 count weighted at 75 percent with the 2020-2021 count weighted at 25 percent, multiplied by the foundation allowance per pupil to determine total foundation funding.

**MPSERS cost support.** Contributions are computed as a percentage of payroll and the required rate continues to increase. The estimated 2020-2021 contribution rate ranged from 35.47 to 42.72 percent, and the rate net of state funding support paid directly by the employer ranged from 20.96 to 28.21 percent. State support flows through Sections 147a, 147c, and 147e of the State Aid Act. Troy received $1,070,809 in 147a1, $1,838,621 in 147a2, $11,658,202 in 147c1, and $206,687 of 147e. Total retirement contributions represent approximately 42 percent of covered payroll recognized as expenditure, with the district responsible for approximately a 28 percent net contribution.

**Coronavirus Relief Fund and other federal funding.** In summer 2020 approximately $362 per pupil was provided to districts by the Michigan Department of Education through summer state aid payments; the total available to Troy was $4,588,959. Because the funding was not approved until July 2020, revenue recognition was deferred to fiscal year 2021, and for the year ended June 30, 2021 the district fully expended the award and recognized the related federal revenue. Two key funding sources are the Education Stabilization Fund (ESF), whose principal programs are the Elementary and Secondary School Emergency Relief (ESSER) Fund and the Governor's Education Emergency Relief (GEER) Fund, and the Coronavirus Relief Fund (CRF), which includes the $362 per pupil passed through by MDE plus amounts from other nonfederal entities. Reimbursement claims could reach back to costs incurred as early as March 2020.

**ESSER awards.** ESSER grants come in three waves: ESSER I, ESSER II (divided between phase 1 and phase 2), and ESSER III. The district's ESSER I award was $246,411; ESSER II and III estimates are $843,258 and $1,893,840 respectively. ESSER I revenue could be recognized in fiscal 2021 to the extent allowable expenditures were incurred. Phase 1 ESSER II revenue could be recognized in fiscal 2021 only if a grant award letter was received by June 30, 2021; many districts did not receive theirs, deferring recognition to fiscal 2022. Phase 2 of ESSER II and ESSER III awards become available in fiscal 2022. ESSER allocations use the Title I model based on economically disadvantaged demographics, so the Legislature and governor established a floor of $450 per pupil for ESSER II with state equalization payments. Based on its ESSER II level, Troy qualified for an equalization payment of $5,036,199, received over the May through August 2021 state aid payments; the district recognized a portion as fiscal 2021 revenue and will recognize the remainder in fiscal 2022. For ESSER III the state set a funding floor of $1,093 per student, but the federal government is now questioning the legality of that state-funded equalization payment.

**2022 funding implications.** The May 2021 Revenue Estimating Conference was optimistic for 2022, 2023, and 2024, projecting the School Aid Fund to close the State's 2021 fiscal year with a fund balance. For 2021-2022 all districts move to the target foundation of $8,700 per pupil; districts already at target receive a $171 per pupil increase from the former target of $8,529, and for hold harmless districts such as Troy the $171 arrives as a $115 per pupil foundation increase plus $56 per pupil of Section 20m funding. Pupil counts revert to the pre-2021 method for 2021-2022, weighted 90 percent fall count and 10 percent spring count. Significant summer 2021 resources supported summer school, credit recovery, and before- and after-school programming through ESSER II plus state aid for innovative summer programming. For 2021-2022 the overall MPSERS contribution rate is expected to increase to 43 percent from 42 percent with the net cost to the district approximating 28 percent.

**Looking forward.** The May 2021 conference projected a 2021 surplus carrying into 2022 with surpluses expected in 2023 and 2024. Factors to monitor include the economic bounce back, the tail-off of federal stimulus over the next two years, the success of returning to in-class instruction, learning loss, enrollment changes, personnel shortages, staffing cost increases, and retirement system cost trends. The next Revenue Estimating Conference will occur in January 2022.

**Grants management and budgeting.** Pandemic programs such as ESSER, GEER, and CRF have increased workload and grants management risk across superintendents and leadership, board members, the business office, staff, information technology, support services, procurement, and facilities. The firm suggests performing a risk assessment of key processes and controls in fiscal 2022. Federal funds carry program end dates laddered through 2024 and are nonrecurring, so recurring uses will require redirecting other revenue or discontinuing programs. Recommended budget practices include multiyear revenue forecasting, monitoring pupil counts, separating recurring contractual payroll costs from variable payroll costs funded by pandemic resources, and budgeting one-time uses of federal and state assistance.

**MPSERS plan net liabilities.** The MPSERS plan has a September 30 year end. At September 30, 2020 the pension portion had a net pension liability of approximately $35 billion, an increase from $33.8 billion at September 30, 2019, about 3.5 percent, driven primarily by less favorable actuarial experience than assumed. The retiree health care (OPEB) portion had a net OPEB liability of approximately $5.4 billion at September 30, 2020, down from $7.3 billion at September 30, 2019, a decrease of approximately 26 percent, reflecting a reduction in the health care cost trend rate from 7.5 percent to 7.0 percent and favorable experience from lower than projected health benefit costs.

**Fund balance.** During 2020-2021 the district's General Fund revenue exceeded expenditures by approximately $6,700,000, increasing General Fund fund balance to approximately $32,700,000 at June 30, 2021. The statewide average for school districts at June 30, 2020 was approximately 15.90 percent of expenditures, equal to about an eight-week operating period; the School District's fund balance percentage is 19.88 percent and equals approximately 10.3 weeks of operation. Rising CPI and decisions about spending COVID-19 relief funds are cited as pressures on 2021-2022 fund balance.

**Cybersecurity and IT.** Education remains a top ransomware target. The "Enhancing K-12 Cybersecurity Act" was introduced in the House in June 2021 and would appropriate $10M yearly for two years to improve district cybersecurity. The letter warns that weak passwords such as "August2021" are easily guessed, raises questions about data location, PII and FERPA data on file-sharing sites or flash drives, and recommends an external vulnerability assessment. It also recommends an IT assessment covering governance, IT staff and organization, external service providers, service delivery, network and device management, cybersecurity policies, and the technology itself, noting many districts use the results as a two- to three-year action plan.

**Accounting and auditing standards ahead.** GASB Statement No. 87, Leases, is effective for the district's June 30, 2022 financial statements and requires lessees to recognize a lease liability and intangible right-of-use asset and lessors to recognize a lease receivable and deferred inflow, with new disclosures; the district must inventory all lease contracts and embedded leases. SAS No. 134, Auditor Reporting and Amendments, issued by the AICPA Auditing Standards Board in May 2019, takes effect for the June 30, 2022 audited financial statements and moves the opinion to the top of the letter, expands the basis of opinion section, explains materiality, defines reasonable assurance, notes that fraud risk exceeds error risk, enhances going concern reporting, describes auditor responsibilities, and introduces key audit matters. The GASB financial reporting model project began in August 2013 with an exposure draft, "Financial Reporting Model Improvements," issued in June 2020; the comment period ended in February 2021, Plante & Moran submitted comments, and final standards are targeted by June 2022. Proposed changes include additional MD&A information, a budget-to-actual variance column between original and amended budget, terminology shifts from "revenue" and "expenditures" to "inflows" and "outflows of resources," and replacement of modified accrual with a "short-term financial resources measurement focus" using a 12-month horizon rather than the current 60-day receivable rule. Adoption is phased: districts with total annual revenue across all funds over $75 million adopt for the year ending June 30, 2025, and those under $75 million for the year ending June 30, 2026. A related GASB project, the June 2020 preliminary views on "Revenue and Expense Recognition," could produce a standard during 2025.

2021_217_boe_shared_copy_program_facilit.paragraph: Facilities Condition & Program Assessment Report presented to the Troy School District Board of Education on October 5, 2021, following a study that kicked off in March 2021 and toured facilities through August 2021. The condition assessment inventoried roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings averaging 48 years of age on approximately 500 acres, and priced identified needs at $220-250 Million across roofing, architectural, mechanical, electrical, site work, furniture and kitchen equipment, buses, and technology devices. A 57-member Facilities Review Committee was to first meet October 12th, with an update at the December 7th Board workshop.
2021_217_boe_shared_copy_program_facilit.page:
**Presentation.** "Facilities Condition & Program Assessment Report," Troy School District, presented to the Board of Education under the agenda item "BOE Shared Copy Program & Facilities Assessment Report." The team included the cabinet, administrators, staff, students, and parents.

**Two areas of focus.** The Facilities Condition Assessment covered interior and exterior infrastructure and sites against code and standards, sorted into categories of 1-3, 4-6, 7-10, 10+, and 15+ years. The Program Assessment identified barriers and deficiencies in buildings and sites that impede delivering education in the most optimum way today and in the future.

**Process.** Kick-off meeting March 2021; facilities toured March through August 2021; status meetings; project worklists developed; items quantified and cost estimates developed; needs categorized and prioritized.

**Fun facts.** Roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, over 50 acres; approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures; over 4,300 doors; over 2 million square feet of parking lot; 1.7 million square feet of roofing; average building age 48 years; approximately 500 acres of property, roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**System findings and cost ranges.** Roofing, with a typical 20-year lifespan and aging roofs, $10-15 Million. Architectural systems, covering aging doors, flooring, and furnishings such as cabinets, gym equipment, and marker boards, $40-45 Million. Mechanical systems, with a 20-year equipment lifespan, aging boilers, aging classroom unit ventilators, and malfunctioning plumbing fixtures, $45-50 Million. Electrical systems, including LED lighting upgrades with energy rebates and operational savings and replacement of emergency/exit lighting, $30-35 Million, illustrated with existing and new lighting in the Troy High School Media Center. Site work paving, with a 20-year asphalt lifespan, replacing aging parking lots and sidewalks, $20-23 Million. Playgrounds and athletics, assessed on condition, age appropriateness, and safety, $5-7 Million.

**Cost summary by category.**

| Item | Cost range |
| --- | --- |
| Roofing Systems | $10-15 Million |
| Architectural Systems | $40-45 Million |
| Mechanical Systems | $45-50 Million |
| Electrical Systems | $30-35 Million |
| Site Work | $25-30 Million |
| Furniture, Kitchen Equipment | $23-28 Million |
| Buses | $12 Million |
| Technology Devices | $35 Million |
| **Total** | **$220-250 Million** |

**Cost summary by priority.**

| Item | Cost range |
| --- | --- |
| Critical Needs (1-3 years) | $45-55 Million |
| Near Future Needs (4-6 years) | $90-100 Million |
| Future Needs (7-10 years) | $85-95 Million |
| **Total** | **$220-250 Million** |

**Program assessment.** Program decisions can absorb facilities needs, and the program assessment carries no dollar amount, which comes later in design work. Steps were vision setting and discovery, defining the ideal program, and evaluating existing schools against that ideal. Leaders cited making thinking visible, the 6 C's of learning (collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, character/compassion, citizenship), project-based learning, competency-based learning, social emotional learning, multi-tiered systems of supports, and experiential learning through internships, career pathways, and CTE. Teachers named team collaborative work, one-on-one time, mobile technology, and workshop instruction, and valued good lighting, natural light, and decluttered, flexible space. Among secondary students, 85.7% agree that more connections to real-life experiences should be provided. A workshop with Dr. Tony Wagner explored deep learning, its barriers (money, resources, time; staff and parent readiness; physical structure and furniture; state mandated credits and time requirements), and its ideal space.

**Attributes and guiding principles.** Every school is documented in spreadsheet format with detailed notes for review by the Facilities Review Committee, graded Good, Needs Improvement, or Poor on attributes including smaller learning communities, classroom size, ability to adapt, collaboration spaces, connection to the outdoors, entry image, traffic separation on site, appropriate playgrounds, teacher collaboration spaces, spaces for physical activities, athletic/recreation/community facilities, spaces for fine and performing arts, spaces for community partnerships, universal design, acoustics, environmental control, natural light, integration of technology, and mobile and varied furniture. Guiding principles address curiosity and movement, safe and welcoming access, gross motor development, smaller learning communities, flexible spaces, abundant natural light, eco-friendly schools, professional space for staff, district brand image, universal design accessibility, shared collaboration spaces, career exploration and community partnerships, and well-being and sensory needs.

**Next steps.** A 57-member Facilities Review Committee of community members from all areas of the district plus teachers, administrators, and students was to hold its first meeting October 12th, with an update at the BOE Workshop on December 7th. A slide asks "Questions for TMP?"
2021_217_boe_shared_copy_program_facilit.verbose:
Ninety-two-slide presentation titled "Facilities Condition & Program Assessment Report" for Troy School District, brought to the Board of Education meeting of October 5, 2021 under the agenda title "BOE Shared Copy Program & Facilities Assessment Report." The team slide lists cabinet, administrators, staff, students, and parents.

**Two areas of focus.** The Facilities Condition Assessment examined interior and exterior infrastructure and sites, code and standards, using categories of 1-3, 4-6, 7-10, 10+, and 15+. The Program Assessment focused on identifying barriers and deficiencies in the district's school buildings and sites that prevent or impede delivering education in the most optimum way today and in the future.

**Process and agenda.** The condition assessment agenda covered overview, fun facts, facility findings (roofing, architectural, mechanical, electrical, civil, playground/athletics), cost summary, and next steps. The kick-off meeting was held in March 2021, facilities were toured from March through August 2021, status meetings were held, project worklists were developed, items were quantified and cost estimates developed, and needs were categorized and prioritized.

**Fun facts about the district's physical plant.** Roughly 2.2 million square feet of buildings, described as over 50 acres. Approximately 20,000 interior light fixtures. Over 4,300 doors. Over 2 million square feet of parking lot. 1.7 million square feet of roofing. Average building age of 48 years old. Approximately 500 acres of property, described as roughly 2.3% of Troy's total area.

**Roofing.** Typical roof lifespan is 20 years and the district's roofs are aging. Cost range $10-15 Million.

**Architectural systems.** Aging doors, aging flooring, and aging furnishings including cabinets, gym equipment, and marker boards. Cost range $40-45 Million.

**Mechanical systems.** Mechanical equipment lifespan is 20 years; findings include aging boilers, aging classroom unit ventilators, and malfunctioning plumbing fixtures. Cost range $45-50 Million.

**Electrical systems.** Opportunities include energy rebates and operational savings, upgrading lighting to energy efficient LED, and replacing emergency and exit lighting. Cost range $30-35 Million. Before-and-after images show Troy High School Media Center existing lighting and Troy High Media Center new lighting.

**Site work, paving.** Typical lifespan of asphalt is 20 years; recommendations are to replace aging parking lots and replace sidewalks. Cost range $20-23 Million.

**Site work, playgrounds and athletics.** Assessment completed based on condition, age appropriateness, and safety. Cost range $5-7 Million.

**Cost summary by category.** Roofing Systems $10-15 Million; Architectural Systems $40-45 Million; Mechanical Systems $45-50 Million; Electrical Systems $30-35 Million; Site Work $25-30 Million; Furniture, Kitchen Equipment $23-28 Million; Buses $12 Million; Technology Devices $35 Million; total $220-250 Million.

**Cost summary by priority.** Critical Needs (1-3 years) $45-55 Million; Near Future Needs (4-6 years) $90-100 Million; Future Needs (7-10 years) $85-95 Million; total $220-250 Million.

**Program assessment framing.** The presentation stresses the interplay between facilities needs and program needs, noting that some program decisions may impact and "take care of" facilities needs; the example given is that design of a new instructional space will address the need to update lighting and architectural systems. The program assessment is not accompanied by a dollar amount, which comes in design work moving forward. The sequence is vision setting and discovery, understanding TSD vision and goals and looking to the future of education, defining the ideal program, and evaluating existing schools against the ideal future program of spaces.

**Feedback shared by leaders.** Themes include making thinking visible; the 6 C's of learning - collaboration, communication, critical thinking, creativity, character/compassion, and citizenship; motivating learners to explore information in order to construct new ideas, identify new relationships, and create new models of thinking and behavior; dream and imagination; project based learning leveraging real-world partnerships, scenarios and applications; descriptive grading and alternative assessment; character education; responsive/workshop instruction; social emotional learning; multi-tiered system of supports and the "whole child"; growth mindset; experiential learning through internships, career pathways and CTE; competency based learning with mastery learning and self-paced flexibility; and authentic learning or learning by doing.

**What teachers reported.** Top instructional practices were team collaborative work, one on one with teacher, learning with mobile technology, social emotional learning, independent study, performance based learning, project-based learning, workshop, peer-to-peer, and classroom libraries. Students are most engaged when emotional well-being is prioritized, content extends to students' lives, there is collaboration with peers, opportunities for choice, readily accessible resources, curiosity is piqued, students can see effort paying off, and individualized expectations are visible. Attributes that make a teacher want to be in a space are good lighting, natural light, clean and decluttered, inspiring, active and allowing movement, connection to others, and flexibility to change the space.

**Elementary student responses.** To be successful students said it is important to work well as a team, be creative, and think about hard questions and solve big problems. They learn best working quietly on their own, talking to other students about what they are learning, building projects together, and when they feel happy, and ranked learning with friends, with their teacher, and with their family in that order of importance.

**Secondary student responses.** Interest in going to school is affected by subject matter connecting to interests, fun activities, choosing where and how to work best, opportunities to develop talents, comfortable environments, confidence from succeeding, awareness of expectations, feeling safe to explore ideas without fear of failure, opportunities to work alone, and a flexible class schedule. 85.7% agree that more connections to real-life experiences should be provided to students. Spaces that positively impact learning are social commons, flexible learning studios, partnership space where real life skills can be shared, private space, outdoor spaces, and lab/maker spaces; students are most comfortable with soft comfortable furniture, clean and de-cluttered rooms, access to food and drink throughout the day, and quiet and calm space.

**Dr. Tony Wagner workshop.** Administrators answered five questions. On the most important characteristics of deep learning: inquiry and project based learning; collaboration and feedback; critical thinking with access to resources, tools and technology; foundational feelings of safety and connection to topic; student voice, agency and exhibition; and learning from failure. On activities that lead to deep learning: working collaboratively on a team, encouraging creativity and thinking outside the box, demonstrating, challenging and defending ideas, and spaces and access to research. On current barriers or roadblocks: money, resources and time; preparing staff and parents for change, culture shift and buy in; the physical structure of the building and furniture; state mandated credits and time requirements; and the current system's mindset, tradition and risk tolerance. On the ideal space: flexible and moveable, more natural light, calming colors and tones with students first and safety, a "watering hole" place to collaborate, places for students to showcase work, and space allowing collaboration of students and staff from multiple disciplines. On what success looks like: evidence of student engagement, inspiring future learning, students feeling passionate and finding meaning and purpose, other schools coming to learn from Troy, relationships developing between students and staff, and everyone feeling comfortable sharing ideas.

**Attributes of modern learning environments.** Every school is documented in spreadsheet format with detailed notes for review by the Facilities Review Committee, with a program assessment grade across all buildings and all attributes rated Good, Needs Improvement, or Poor. Attributes assessed include smaller learning communities (systematic organization of spaces sized for a small subset of the school population, adjacency supporting seamless movement and non-traditional schedules, and a menu of spaces encouraging subject-matter cross fertilization); classroom size (space for flexible furniture and student movement, project-based, peer-to-peer and student-centered learning); ability to adapt (spaces easily adapted for current and future programs, with technology and infrastructure supporting fast delivery shifts); collaboration spaces (adjacent to instructional spaces, configured for passive supervision, organized with variety of group size, horizontal surface size and content sharing); connection to the outdoors; entry image (clearly visible and branded secure entry, visible inside and outside, directing visitors to staff/help, consistent brand); traffic separation on site (separate bus and parent drop off, safe traffic flow, dedicated visitor parking, dedicated entrances for academics, athletics and performing arts); appropriate playgrounds (safe and sustainable materials, accessibility, supporting active bodies); teacher collaboration spaces assigned to specific Professional Learning Communities; spaces for physical activities accessible in all weather and supporting social emotional and wellness goals including formal gym class and wellness uses such as meditation and yoga; athletic, recreation and community facilities (safe and in good condition, practice and match/game space, adequate size for players and spectators, equity across genders, easily secured for community use, addressing recreation as well as athletics); spaces for fine and performing arts with practice, gallery and performance space; spaces for community partnerships affording real-life training, accessible to industry professionals and after-hours use, with partnership branding opportunities; universal design; acoustics (surface materials lowering sound reverberation time, reduced background noise, improved speech intelligibility, mechanical systems designed to reduce background noise, and intentional quiet/isolation spaces); environmental control (on demand temperature, ventilation and air quality adjustability, varied lighting solutions with adjustable levels and color temperatures, displayed energy use information); natural light (daylit spaces supporting circadian rhythms, energy reduction through daylighting, views supporting creative thinking); integration of technology (students sharing content from devices, content clearly visible to all learners); and mobile, varied furniture that is easily reconfigured, inclusive of all body sizes and abilities, and encourages movement.

**Guiding principles.** Provide spaces that encourage curiosity, movement and exploration; convenient, direct, safe and welcoming access for students and parents; interior and exterior spaces for gross motor development; organize schools into smaller learning communities supporting belonging, collaboration, inclusion and equity; provide flexible, adaptable and stimulating learning spaces; provide abundant natural light in all instructional spaces; make schools eco-friendly with interaction with the natural environment; provide professional space for teachers and staff to encourage teaming, collaboration, interaction and observation; create a strong, progressive, inviting and innovative visual image promoting the district brand; ensure accessibility for all students and staff through universal design; provide shared collaboration spaces for individual, small group and large groups; create spaces for career exploration and community partnerships supporting real-world experiential learning; design spaces supporting well-being including quiet and sensory spaces; create spaces for interdisciplinary collaboration; provide flexible furnishings to transform existing classrooms into flexible learning studios; improve shared spaces for fine and performing arts, athletics and other performances and competitions for students and the community; assure seamless integration of technology; and transform existing playgrounds into outdoor spaces reinforcing curricular goals and a positive relationship with nature.

**Next steps.** A slide asks "Questions for TMP?" The Facilities Review Committee will have 57 members drawn from community members from all areas of the district plus teachers, administrators, and students. Its first meeting is October 12th, with an update to be given at the BOE Workshop on December 7th.
